layman_trigger: Fine — suppose you're even right about the harm. 'Do not procreate' still can't be willed as universal law: followed by everyone, it ends the whole moral community, leaving no agents to hold, teach, or be bound by any rule at all. A maxim that abolishes the preconditions of morality itself fails Kant's test on form alone — the view is self-effacing, whatever its content.
layman_gloss: Recasts a rule's success condition — universal keeping empties its own scope — as a logical defect. Kant's test finds no contradiction there, and 'no holders left' was never one.
layman_win_line: A rule everyone keeps to the end has succeeded, not contradicted itself.
layman_diagnosis: Kant's test finds no contradiction. False promising eats the practice it needs; 'no one procreates' eats nothing — no concept breaks, only a headcount; a last generation can keep the rule to the end. The structure proves too much: any morality merely permitting universal childlessness lands there too, so singling this view out needs a duty to procreate or 'an empty world is bad' — the value claim it swore off. Unheld isn't unholdable: finished rules retire, eradication protocols do, and truths outlive their last believer. What's left — 'a will must will agency onward' — isn't logic but the old claim that existence is good, answered elsewhere.
